cues.text: Chapter two: Quality attributes and auditability.
Let us begin with the quality model your course uses.
It is the ISO/IEC 25010 product quality model.
A note on terminology first: the course commonly uses the earlier terminology of this standard.
Newer revisions update the terminology and the characteristics, so you should be careful to distinguish what the syllabus model says from any assertion about what the current edition says.
When you write about this in an answer, attribute the list to the syllabus model, and do not claim it describes the current edition.
In that model, product quality includes eight characteristics.
They are functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, and portability.
Say them again slowly, because examiners like to ask for the full list: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, portability.
Now let us look at several of these in more detail, as the source describes them.
Maintainability, in the earlier model, includes five sub-characteristics: modularity, analysability, modifiability, testability, and reusability.
Usability concerns effective, efficient, and satisfying interaction.
Notice what this implies.
Functionality can be correct, and yet the interface can still be difficult to use.
A system can do exactly what it was specified to do and still frustrate the people using it.
Those are two separate qualities.
Reliability covers availability, fault tolerance, and recoverability.
Availability is about whether the system is there when needed.
Fault tolerance is about continuing to operate when faults occur.
Recoverability is about getting back to a working state afterwards.
Security includes confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity or accountability, along with other attributes under the model.

The source names these three explicitly and leaves the rest under the general heading, so when you write about security, name confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity or accountability, and you may say there are other attributes under the model.
Now to the second block: how we assess these attributes.
The key principle is this: assess attributes separately.
They are different qualities, and a good result in one does not tell you about another.
The source gives three examples.
First, an ERP system, that is an enterprise resource planning system, which requires broad edits for every tax change.
That system has weak modifiability.
A tax rule changes, and instead of one contained change, you must edit widely across the system.
The cost of change is high, and modifiability, part of maintainability, is the attribute that is weak.
Second, a correct learning app with confusing navigation.
The app does what it should, so its functionality is correct, but the navigation confuses the learner.
That is a usability issue, not a functional one.
Third, maintainable code does not guarantee a usable product.
The code might be well organised and easy for developers to change, yet the people using the product may still find it hard to use.
Maintainability and usability are assessed separately.
How should you assess them?
Express measurable criteria.
A vague aim such as "easy to use" cannot be tested, so state a criterion that can be measured.
Then test with representative users and operational conditions.
That means the people who will really use the system, and the conditions it will really run under, not only ideal laboratory conditions.
Finally, the source turns to auditability, specifically forensic audit evidence.
If logs are to serve as evidence, several practices are needed.
Protect logs from tampering.
Control access to them.
Record timestamps, identity, and action, so that each entry shows when something happened, who did it, and what was done.
Establish chain of custody, so you can show who held the evidence and that it was not altered.
And set retention, so that records are kept for the required period.
Tamper-evident or append-only logs support integrity and accountability.
Append-only means entries are added but not rewritten.
Tamper-evident means that alteration can be detected.
But remember the qualification the source makes: these measures support integrity and accountability, they are not infallible.
Do not claim that such a log makes evidence perfect or beyond dispute.
It strengthens the evidence; it does not guarantee it.

To pull the chapter together: know the eight characteristics from the syllabus model, remember the caution about newer revisions, assess each attribute separately with measurable criteria and representative users and conditions, and when logs are forensic evidence, protect, control, timestamp, attribute,
preserve custody, and retain, while staying honest that the logs are supportive, not infallible.
